The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Kaplan that Bill C-9, an Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, to enact an Act respecting enforcement in relation to certain security and related offences and to amend certain acts in consequence thereof or in relation thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in addressing my remarks to Bill C-9, when we adjourned at one o'clock 1 was stating that with any piece of legislation which deals with intelligence gathering and surveillance of individuals, first and foremost one must see that any necessary constraints and limitations are placed on the activities of the agency itself and not allow the powers of that agency to abuse or violate the basic rights and freedoms of Canadian. That should be basic to this Bill or any others of a similar nature.
Does this Bill meet that particular objective? Certainly it is an improvement over its predecessor, Bill C-157, but in my mind it still leaves a great deal to be desired. Let me illustrate what I mean. The Bill deals with the powers of investigation assigned to the new agency. Clause 21 states:
Where the Director or any employee designated by the Minister for the purpose believes, on reasonable grounds, that a warrant under this section is required to enable the Service to investigate a threat to the security of Canada or to perform its duties and functions under section 16, the Director or employee may, after having obtained the approval of the Minister, make an application in accordance with subsection (2) to a judge for a warrant under this section.
As a result, Federal Court justices would issue warrants for intrusive techniques such as electronic surveillance, mail opening and access to confidential information. Certain things would not be allowed, such as information under the Statistics Act. Nevertheless, the issuance of that warrant to carry out these particular techniques is, from my point of view, a dangerous provision for several reasons.
Nowhere in the Act, Mr. Speaker, is it clearly defined when a warrant might be granted. Words such as "espionage" and "sabotage" are used, but their meaning is not clearly outlined anywhere in the Bill. Therefore one has to ask how a judge would decide when to issue a warrant without a legal definition from which to proceed. It is the duty and responsibility of this House to pass laws which contain those definitions. Surely, Sir, it is Parliament, not the courts, which is the maker of laws.
Since such crucial words as "sabotage" and "espionage" are not defined, it is surely easy to see why so many people are concerned about this Bill. Groups, organizations and associations like the Civil Liberties Association are campaigning against this Bill. They are concerned about it. They rightly point out that almost any group in Canada would be investigated if the Government disagreed with their objectives and activities. That could extend to activities they might carry out on behalf of individuals in this country or in different parts of the world.
The Solicitor General has tried to argue that the Minister must have the right to judge when the gravity of this threat to security supersedes the need to violate the privacy of those affected when deciding to make an application for a warrant. He puts the one against the other and says he should have the right to decide when the gravity of the threat to security is the more important.
February 13, 1984

That is a very dangerous instrument in the hands of any individual. If I could be assured that every Minister opposite and any Minister at any time had the wisdom of Solomon, was totally honest and incapable of error, then perhaps that proposal could be given some consideration. I know and you know, Sir, that such is not the case. Nowhere has this been better illustrated than in the last few days with the bungling of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres), or in the recent letter episode carried on by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). Those examples painfully illustrate the abusive powers that this particular piece of legislation could be turned into.
Those two examples show that it is never the Ministers who have to bear the consequences of the act when government authority is abused; it is those who are the butt of their abuse who needlessly suffer.
One can also look at the negative effects the abusive tactics of Revenue Canada have had on the lives of hundreds of average Canadians. We can imagine the anguish, the anxiety and the despair to which many of them have been subjected. That is power in the hands of a Minister of the Crown. That is power in the hands of a Minister of the Crown when, as the Minister of Finance did recently, he used his office and information which he had in confidence to make statements against the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney)-statements which he could not later substantiate, simply because we have a Minister of Finance more concerned with politics than with justice.
Furthermore, if one were to look at the potential for abuse, one need look no further than the infamous case of Peter Treu. Here was a Canadian on whom information was collected in secret; he was charged in secret and his trial was held in secret. In his case all the basic rules of justice were disregarded-the basic rules such as being innocent until guilt is proven and the right to face your accusers. Those things were disregarded. He was eventually cleared of all charges, nevertheless his reputation, his job, his savings and his personal life were all wrecked because of far-reaching powers which were beyond the rule of law.
Examples like these frighten me and frighten a lot of Canadians, Mr. Speaker. They show that a single Minister ought not to be given the sole responsibility of directing an agency which has such extensive powers as the one presently proposed will have.
It has been correctly said that information is power. I believe that no single Minister ought to have the power over people's lives that this Bill seeks to assign. There simply are not the checks and balances that we need. The Solicitor General has argued that case and has said that the abuse of power would be impossible as the agency would be subjected to civilian review by three different bodies. He thinks those are sufficient checks and balances.
The first of these bodies which would review the power of the agency is the Inspector General, who would review the operational activities of the service and monitor its compliance with operational policies. As such, we are told that the Inspec-
Security Intelligence Service
tor General is allowed access to all information that the service has, except for Cabinet documents. I ask you, Sir, how can the Inspector General monitor the activities of the service and ensure compliance when he will be unable to see the Cabinet document which may affect the service? This is particularly important since the Minister has direct control over the service and must authorize all applications for warrants.
If this implication were not so serious, one would almost have to laugh at such a provision. As far as 1 can see, the Inspector General would be a watchdog without teeth. He would never have all the necessary information at his disposal.
I would say that the same situation holds true for the second monitoring body, the Security Intelligence Review Committee. It would generally review the performance by the service of its duties and functions under the Act. That would be its responsibility. As well, it would investigate complaints, hold hearings dealing with security assessments and file reports with the Minister in Parliament. However, once again Cabinet documents are not included as part of the information to which the committee would have access. Thus, once again the effectiveness of the committee is limited as it will never have all the facts.
Finally, the Bill would provide for a third group. It would provide for a review of the substance and operation of the new service by a parliamentary committee five years after proclamation-five years after proclamation, Mr. Speaker. What this sounds like to me is very much like closing the barn door after the horses have escaped.
We have three steps which the Minister has set up which he says will eliminate the potential for any abuse under the Bill. Sir, I do not believe that they have the necessary power. As in cases like this, there is a very fine balance between the threat to security and the right to privacy of every individual. That is what we are talking about here. While Bill C-9 comes much closer to achieving that balance than did its predecessor, Bill C-157, nevertheless I feel it is far from satisfactory in this regard.
The language in the Bill is ill-defined. It leaves the door open to unnecessary and to potentially dangerous abuse. There is far too much in the way of discretionary powers given to the Minister and to the Cabinet. It assigns far-reaching powers to the agency but provides far from adequate provisions for the monitoring of the agency's activities.
The rule of law has always been one of the linchpins of our system of government. This Bill would create conditions which would violate those principles. For this reason, Members on this side of the House simply cannot with a clear conscience permit the Bill to pass in its present form.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I listened with care to the thoughtful remarks of the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). I share many of the concerns she has expressed. I should like to ask a specific

Security Intelligence Service
question about one element that the Hon. Member highlighted and that is the question of oversight and accountability.
The Hon. Member will know that the McDonald Commission strongly recommended the establishment of a small parliamentary oversight committee made up of members of the Opposition to ensure that ultimately the new security service would be accountable to Parliament and not just to a specific Minister and a hand appointed body by the Minister of the day. I should like to ask the Hon. Member whether she supports the establishment of a parliamentary committee to oversee the operations of the new security service as recommended by the McDonald Commission.

Mr. Speaker, I say to the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) that I am very sympathetic to that particular proposal. I would want to make sure, however, that it is truly an independent parliamentary committee and not one which has been co-opted by the Minister of the day to serve his or her purposes.
I take it, then, that the Hon. Member would agree with the appointment of such a committee providing that these safeguards for independence were in fact met. Is that correct?

Yes, certainly, and I would like to examine it. As I am sure the Hon. Member knows, there are certain other jurisdictions in other countries which have such a set-up. 1 would like us take a look at them and see what are the best aspects of this kind of operation in other countries which we could bring into our own system.

Mr. Speaker, I was likewise very interested in the remarks of the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), in particular her comments with respect to the imprecision and inadequacies of the Bill. Will the Hon. Member tell us whether she and her Party will be preparing for the committee, when it meets, a series of amendments which will put into precise form the exact wording she would like to see in the Bill so that we can judge whether those proposed amendments in fact accomplish our ends more effectively than the words which are in the present Bill?

Mr. Speaker, I would say to the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) that we have a lot of difficulty with this Bill. We do think it should be much more precise. However, I do not feel at this point we should say "Here are the amendments we suggest". We feel there are a great many people in this country who have something to contribute to the definitions which should go into this Bill. They have not all been heard from as yet, by any means. After we hear what they have to say, I would invite the Hon. Member to come along to the committee and listen to the amendments which we will be presenting.

Mr. Speaker, I also want to congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands
(Miss MacDonald), for another first-rate contribution in this particular debate. She is always germane and always speaking on behalf of the interests of the average citizen in our country. She did not disappoint us with respect to this important issue.
In connection with the matter which she raised with respect to the amendments in the committee-and the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) has alluded to this-Hon. Members and the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) I am sure will be happy to know that we are prepared to come forward with specific and precise recommendations by way of amendments to the existing legislation. I feel that there has been an enormous amount of time spent on drafting the predecessor Bill and this Bill, and, unfortunately, it still is not right.
I have tried to bring out some points with respect to the preposterous conclusions, as I see them, which one arrives at regarding the present definition of "threats to national security". The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East, as a former Solicitor General, will understand that these are difficult and complex issues. However, the opportunity has now been given to us. After 15 years of a subject being considered by a variety of commissions and a Senate committee, we in the House of Commons, the elected representatives of the people of Canada, now have an opportunity for input. We take our responsibility seriously.
I ask rhetorically of the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East whether or not he wants to support legislation which gives a mandate to the security service to obtain information with respect to people who support Solidarity in Poland, who support the Afghan rebels, who support the Sandinista rebels in Central America? This is the conclusion one has to come to if one studies clearly a definition of the threat to the security of Canada. We have concerns and apprehensions with respect to these definitions. We will be up front. We will be there with our amendments and proposals at the appropriate time. However, these are the issues which have to be discussed on the floor of the House of Commons. We have had a lot of different proposals brought forward leading to the present Bill. There have been a number of changes. But it is too facile for a person to stand up and say "Let's shut our eyes and move ahead", without reasonable and adequate consideration and deliberation.
I simply want to assure Hon. Members of this House that, as far as amendments are concerned, we are considering them and we will in fact be doing our duty as loyal Members of Her Majesty's Opposition.

I know he was from Scotland but somehow he went to Montreal after he left the West and a lot of people identify him with the Acting Speaker's part of the world.
I would like to start with the theme which was raised by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands
Security Intelligence Service
(Miss MacDonald). The problem that we on this side of the House have is that the predecessor Bill was so bad. 1 think most Hon. Members on this side would concede that this Bill is considerably better than the last one. Bill C-157 would qualify for an entry in Ripley's Believe It or Not or the Guiness World Book of Records for perhaps the most draconian piece of legislation ever introduced in the House of Commons. It was so bad that the Government did not have the courage to introduce it in the House. They took it through the Chamber down the hall. It was properly ripped to shreds by one and all who appeared before the Senate committee to deal with it.
My role here today is simply to indicate some of the matters which will be brought out by Members on this side as causing concern if the Bill gets to committee. Starting at the beginning, Section 12(2) in the Bill basically says that the security service is not restricted from "remaining informed through public sources" about the political, economic and social environment within Canada. On this side of the House we would ask why the Senate recommendation was not followed in this respect. If, as the Senate said, the words in the Bill of which 1 am speaking are unnecessary, why are they still in the Bill? Perhaps the Minister will be kind enough to clarify that at an early point.
A little farther on in the definition section of the Bill before us it says that threats to the security of Canada are to be defined as "espionage or sabotage against Canada or any state allied or associated with Canada". On this side of the House we ask why it is that espionage and sabotage were not defined in the Bill we have now. It is true that sabotage is defined in the Criminal Code. Is that the definition that is intended in this Bill? Hon. Members will be curious about that too. We wonder why the term "espionage" is not defined in this Bill. What does the word "espionage" mean? The dictionary definition is essentially spying. Yet spying, according to Section 3 of the Official Secrets Act, is very broadly defined. I ask the Minister why espionage is not defined in the Bill.
The third point I would raise is that the predecessor Bill defined unacceptable behaviour as constituting, among other things, the threat or use of acts of violence against persons or property, and so on. Does throwing a tomato at a politician constitute an act of violence? I am sure most of us in this Chamber have had something thrown at us, if not a tomato. We will take the position in committee that the definition is too broad. A term such as "strictly necessary" should be used in the Bill, as was recommended by the Senate committee. Many provincial attorneys general voiced concern about this part of the Bill, feeling that that definition was too broad. Several witnesses before the Senate Committee urged the Government to change the definition to deal only with threat or use of serious violence, such acts as would not involve the throwing of a tomato at a politician.
My fourth point deals again with the definition of subversive behaviour. The previous Bill defines this as activities directed toward the undermining by covert unlawful acts directed

February 13, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
toward or intended ultimately to lead to the destruction or overthrow of the constitutionally established system of government in Canada. What does this say about legitimate dissent or protest? Witnesses before the Senate committee stated that subversion should not be a concern of the security service but rather should remain a matter for investigation under the Criminal Code.
The fifth matter I would like to deal with is the section dealing with international affairs and defence. In the old Bill it is Section 18. The new section is essentially the same but incorporates the Senate recommendations, except for the suggestion that the service have a monopoly on operational work respecting this type of intelligence gathering. That is Section 16. The question will be asked in committee as to whether the service should be engaged in this type of work which is not directly linked to the security of Canada. It will be asked what the parameters of this provision are. Testimony before the Senate committee said that this section will be used to gather economic, commercial, social and other data about other nations. It is important to note that warrants can be used to allow the service to use techniques for this section. We ask how the judge determines whether to issue a warrant. Does it consist of a security service agent walking into a judge's office and asking him if he would mind signing a warrant which has been approved by the Solicitor General? What a judge will consider and under what circumstances a judge will issue a warrant are serious questions.
The sixth point, Mr. Speaker, is the question of Section 21, which deals with warrants and states a number of things. For example, a provision is added to stipulate that an application for a warrant can only be made with the approval of a Minister. Safeguards or guidelines mentioned by the Senate are to be incorporated. We think that is a good thing. The maximum time limit for a warrant is one year. Confidential records kept pursuant to the Statistics Act, such as census forms, are not subject to warrants. Again it is a question of balancing the gravity of the threat to security and the right of the citizen to privacy.
The Government takes the position that if the Minister has to approve the application for a warrant, he or she will only do so if the circumstances justify such a step. With respect to the maximum period of a warrant, the McDonald Commission recommended a maximum period of 180 days. In this Bill the maximum period is a year. Questions will be asked as to why the McDonald Commission maximum has been so exceeded.
With respect to the Statistics Act, we ask why it is that Statistics Act material is now exempt under the Bill, whereas it was subject to warrant under the previous Bill. We ask whether there should be an annual report on warrant activities such as there is with respect to the Official Secrets Act.
The seventh subject matter I would like to deal with is the question of Section 20. I am talking about the protection of employees. Section 20 states that the Director and employees have the same protection under the law as peace officers. The McDonald Commission recommended that federal and provincial Governments give service employees various exemptions
from specific laws. The question again comes up whether provincial attorneys general who administer the criminal law have the right to information of illegalities committed by the service, perhaps subject to the withholding of certain information if the federal Government believes it to be contrary to the security of Canada to release it. We have concerns in that area.
My eighth point revolves around the question of management control and responsibility. This is obviously an important area. The Bill deletes the provision which gave the director the final word on targets of the service and on information the service would disclose to the Government. If you have had a chance to look at it, you will recall that the present section says that the Minister may issue written instructions to the Director. What about oral directions? How would these come to the attention of the review committee? Should all directions be in writing? If oral directions are sufficient, would there be an incentive for the Minister not to reduce his directions to writing? I hope the Minister will have good answers to those questions when the Bill goes to the Justice Committee.
The ninth concern I would raise relates to Clause 30 which makes it clear that the Inspector General monitors compliance by the service with its operational policies as well as reviewing operational activities.
I am pleased that the Minister is in the House because 1 would like to ask him why the Senate recommendations were not followed in this area. How can the Inspector General monitor the activities of the service and ensure compliance when he will be unable to see Cabinet documents which may affect the service? I ask the Minister to explain that to us at an early date.
My tenth concern relates to Clause 34 which establishes a Security Intelligence Review Committee which would be composed of up to five and not less than three members. Again, the review committee is not allowed access to Cabinet documents in control of the service. How can the committee effectively oversee all the operations of the service when these documents are withheld? The expanded duties of the review committee are set out in line with the Senate report, but I remind the House that the McDonald Commission would have established a joint parliamentary committee to oversee the service.
My last point deals with the question of the Security Offences Act. The RCMP retains primary responsibility but the Solicitor General may enter into arrangements with other police forces respecting the investigation of security offences. The Senate recommendation for the role of the federal Attorney General was followed. In conclusion, I would simply ask if there should be a duty on the part of the RCMP to consult other forces, as the Senate committee suggested?
The concern which has been expressed by other Members is that this matter has dragged on for 15 years. In that time there have been several royal commissions. There have been problems with morale in the security service as well as problems

with respect to the effectiveness of our security service. Finally, a Bill has been introduced after 15 years.
We on this side believe that we would be derelict in our duty, as the Party which expects to form the next Government when an election is called, if we did not give this Bill reasonably close scrutiny before it goes to the Justice Committee. We put the Government on notice again that we will be giving it very close scrutiny when it comes before the Justice Committee.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member, in his very interesting remarks, made reference to two key elements of this legislation which he indicated were of considerable concern. One was with respect to some of the powers being accorded to this new agency, and the second concerned the element of oversight. We in this Party see those two elements, the unprecedented new powers which are accorded to this agency and the importance of parliamentary oversight, as being two of the most essential elements of any Bill that would establish a new security agency.
Certainly the Solicitor General should be aware that if in fact he wants this Bill to go to committee he should be prepared to consider amendments to those two key elements which the McDonald Commission itself singled out as being the heart of legislation in this area. Certainly this Bill must be carefully studied in committee because we want to examine its elements closely. Let me emphasize those two key elements again. The first is the question of parliamentary oversight and accountability which was seen by the McDonald Commission as being the cornerstone of accountability in a security agency in a democratic society. The second element concerns the use of powers, particularly intrusive powers, against Canadians who are suspected of subversion.
As the Solicitor General will know, it is in this particular area that the McDonald Commission strongly emphasized that intrusive techniques should not in fact be permitted.
Let me ask the Member a question with respect to one of these intrusive techniques. It concerns the matter of opening first class mail. The Member has been quoted on a number of occasions as being in support of giving law enforcement agencies the power to open first class mail. Undoubtedly he will know that the Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) is strongly opposed to granting those powers and that his colleague, the Hon. Member for Durham-Northumberland (Mr. Lawrence), has indicated that he supports extending those powers.

In light of his own comments with respect to granting the power to law enforcement agencies to open first class mail, does he believe that the new security intelligence agency should have the power to open first class mail despite the clear recommendation of the McDonald Commission that it should not have such powers?

Mr. Speaker, how the question relates to the preamble, which took approximately three quarters of the Member's comments, eludes me but I will speak to the last part of the question. It is true that I have personally expressed the opinion that I think that Members of the drug section of our RCMP should be permitted to open letters when they have a strong prima facie case that they contain heroin or cocaine. I stand to be corrected, but to my knowledge there is no other country in the world where the mail could not be opened in such circumstances. I would remind the Hon. Member, who knows this, that the general consensus is that people on heroin commit many of the break and enter offences, thefts and robberies that occur across Canada, particularly in British Columbia. I will not answer my friend' question with respect to the security service because, as he knows, this matter is no longer within my responsibility. Therefore I do not have to answer the question.

First, I would like to reflect briefly on the type and the rate of social change occurring in our society and in the world at large. All those who are interested in the social sciences see the tremendous change in attitude, culture, economic and political forums that have been occurring in the last number of years. There has been a very rapid change in social thinking and customs. We talk about technological change, economic change, social change, cultural change and political change. We see a tremendous amount of human displacement. People who are given training in certain trades are, all of a sudden finding those trades no longer valid today. What about people who have been brought up holding beliefs in a certain cultural milieu and setting who find that many of those cultural beliefs are no longer practised by society as a whole? The coming generation, the first of many generations to come, through the revolution in communications and in television, have a high level of expectation in life and a high level of material expectation. Yet on the other side of the coin we see the ability to satisfy those expectations being decreased. We see the possibilities of massive unemployment in the years ahead. People will not be able to find meaningful work or find a meaningful niche in life.
This is a recipe for social disorder and a situation in which many human beings not being able to fulfil their basic expectations are displaced and will react with anger and, at times, with violence. There have been various surveys conducted. I think of a Decima survey done approximately a year ago that shows the degree to which Canadians have lost faith in the traditional institutions. They have lost faith in Parliament, in law enforcement agencies, in government and in the churches. People have lost faith in the traditional social institutions that used to provide the social glue for society. Those were the institutions that kept us together and formulated and helped bring forth shared basic beliefs and value structures.
I mention all of these because I think they are important when we discuss security legislation such as the legislation before us today. We should have some appreciation of the larger context in which society is moving. I can see how some Members, and obviously some government members, react to this in terms of fear and panic. They feel we must have in place greater police powers to attempt to control and even suppress those social changes. My contention is that you cannot in the end suppress social change. We are living in a world of very fast social change, and no amount of secret police and police activities can really suppress social change.
February 13, 1984

What you can do, of course, in a short period of time is to hold back social change. But, like water building up behind a dam, all this will do is to create a power and a force that at some stage will break through and smash down those forces opposed to an actual historic change occurring.
Not only do we see rapid social change within our own borders but we also see it throughout the world, and we also see rising expectations by most of humanity. Most of humanity will no longer put up with ignorance, starvation and political suppression. People will no longer accept the feudal system in which a few suppress the many. On an international scale, we see rising expectations forcing us to change, which very often ends up in revolution. Those who are in control of power do not allow those changes to occur. They use armies and secret police to suppress those changes. But in the end the will of people cannot be stopped. Through revolution many of these changes will come about so that people will begin to realize the hopes and expectations they have.
The security legislation we have in front of us today, I feel, is an attempt by the Government to try to control social change. It opens up the possibility for the Government to use the secret police to attempt to suppress and stop social change.
The way to help accommodate social change, Mr. Speaker, is to anticipate it and to realize that there will be many people without jobs and the ability to earn income in a meaningful way. The solution to that problem is not more police power but, rather, to be a little more creative and to have some political will to put programs into place so that displaced people will be able to find a meaningful role for themselves in their lives. That is really the solution to social change which Canadians are experiencing.
What we have, Mr. Speaker, I feel is an attempt at suppression. Bill C-9 has three essential elements. It proposes a mandate; it spells out powers; and as well it acts as a type of control over the secret service agency which the Government wishes to establish.
Let me first deal with its general mandate. We have seen that even a Conservative attorney general, like the Attorney General for the Province of Ontario, finds that the definitions in the Bill are still quite dangerous and vague, as he says. He further stated that the definition of national security remained "flabby". Also he was concerned about the reference to foreign-influenced activities, because he is afraid it could be applied to foreign multinational corporations doing business in Canada. 1 understand and sympathize with the Attorney General of the Province of Ontario. Many people involved in civil liberties associations and Hon. Members of the House, both in the Conservative Party and in the New Democratic Party, have expressed fear about the broad definitions. I would not be surprised if many government Members had the same fear in their hearts.
Under the definitions in this Bill, various illegal strikes or activities by Canadians in support of the African National Congress or organizations that may wish to combat the Soviet
Security Intelligence Service
invasion in Afghanistan or organizations that are involved in raising money for resistance groups in El Salvador, could be classified as illegal activities. All the people involved in the support of such organizations could find themselves being snooped upon to the full extent of the power included in the Bill.
For example, the Canadian Farm Survival Association could be considered as having engaged in illegal activities when it saw that high interest rates were forcing farmers into bankruptcy and conducted auctions in farmyards where tractors were sold for $1 or so. In the broad definition, that group could be considered as subversive because there is no doubt its economic activities had political overtones.
That is absolutely false, and you know it.
That Association, could be considered subversive.
That is an insult to the RCMP.

Illegal strikes or walkouts, in the broad definition, could be considered subversive activities because they bring into question the accepted established methods of political and economic solutions in the country. The definitions are so broad that anyone who acts in a direct way against the political and economic power structure in Canada could be defined as being subversive and be snooped upon.
The second area of major concern is the type of powers the Bill allows. Canadian citizens could have their conversations bugged, their mail opened and even have the confidentiality of their confessions with their priests invaded. Their homes could be broken into and searched and their confidential records could be invaded, even though there is not the slightest suggestion that any lawbreaking has occurred. The powers of the Bill are so broad that a fair-minded, average Canadian person must be frightened when he or she looks at what Bill C-9 makes legal.
As I mentioned before, the Bill is not designed to gather information when a law has been broken or a particular law anticipates to be broken and there is some criminal activity involved. It is really an intelligence gathering process. It does not have as its end result the laying of charges against anyone. It is just the gathering of intelligence.
Certainly the United States is more threatened by the acts of terrorists both within its borders and from outside. Its citizens have greater protection than we in Canada, especially if this piece of legislation goes through. In the United States, for example, the FBI has to persuade the judge that there are probable grounds to believe that the suspect or group is engaged in a specified illegal activity. In Bill C-9, our standard for a warrant would be lower. It would be "reasonable grounds", and no particular crime would have to be specified. In the United States also, the judge has to be convinced that an electronic interception will produce evidence of a crime. The Canadian Bill will not tie the interception to the gathering of evidence of criminal activity. In our system a warrant could

February 13, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
be issued that would enable the CSIS to investigate a threat. The definition of what is a threat is so wide open that it could include just about any group. We see awesome powers being given to a civilian authority, with very vague definitions as to what are its mandate and its overall purpose.
A third area begs the question-after we have given this tremendous and awesome power to this group of individuals, what type of check or oversight exists? In terms of the judiciary, not very much. Yes, they have to obtain a judicial warrant before they proceed with an investigation, before they open files, tap telephones or break into homes at any hour of the day or night, but the judge really has nothing to go on because the definitions are so broad that he has no choice but to become a rubber stamp. No reasonable grounds have to be offered to show that a crime is being committed or that in some definite period something illegal is occurring or will occur; nothing like that. It is just the interest of some agent of the Government to have a little more information about what a person does, with whom he corresponds, what are his health records or what are his bank records. There is no judicial check, but rather a judicial rubber stamp.
Then we come to the review committee, and we must ask the question as to how effective it will be. Our claim is that there is not enough control over the CSIS. The review committee has no access to Cabinet documents. A recommendation which was made over and over again, even by Senator Pitfield, was that it should at least have access to Government documents. He recognized that there were many ways for the Cabinet and the security agency to get around the review agency, and that to set up a review committee without allowing it full access to the documents would be hampering it from the start. It really becomes a farce. It becomes window dressing and gives the illusion that the review committee is an actual place, when in fact it does not have the ability to look at all documents pertinent to its review of the intelligence service.
What we have here is another piece of double-think, another piece out of George Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four where the show and the pretense are one thing and the actual reality is indeed something else. The major shortcoming in the Bill in terms of its overview is that Parliament is just a eunuch as far as the security service is concerned. Members of Parliament will not have access in a meaningful way to the deliberations and activities of this organization. The Government can claim that Members of Parliament cannot be trusted like the review agency cannot be trusted; even though it is composed of either former members of Cabinet or members of the Privy Council, it cannot be trusted with all the documents, and Members of Parliament can be trusted even less. So much for the Government's trust in the democratic system. The very reason it is setting up this so-called agency is to protect our democratic system. But it has no belief in the democratic system itself.
One must ask the basic question of why the Government is going ahead with this legislation now. Does the present Criminal Code not give tremendous powers to the RCMP to investigate and prosecute criminal cases? If the Government has any reason to believe that there is a national crisis, that our democratic system is in danger, that we need a special security force to investigate Canadians, to tap their telephones and to break into their homes, it should at least have the decency to tell Parliament what the need is. Instead, we get silence from the Government benches. Not one Government Member today during the debate has stood up and given any explanation as to why we should have this Bill.
Perhaps it is a hypothetical explanation. Perhaps something can occur that would require us to have these powers. I suggest that the Government's thinking in all of this has been hypothetical. When the Minister asks for a judicial warrant, it is not based on a fact but based on a hypothetical case. By the same reasoning, the Government is introducing this legislation based on hypothetical cases rather than on a real need.
The Government can say that that is the McDonald Commission recommended. That argument is a farce. It is 1984 double-think. Yes, McDonald recommended a civilian security agency, but McDonald also recommended a security agency with proper and decent checks to it. The Government has chosen to ignore that totally. McDonald found a serious shortcoming in our existing situation. The Government used that as an excuse to legalize illegal activities.
What the Bill does in the end is to create a legal framework for this and future governments to maintain themselves in power through undemocratic means. The very instrument designed to protect our democracy, free speech, judicial system and way of life becomes the very instrument to destroy our democracy, free speech, judicial system, customs and way of life. This is a bad Bill. It stinks. The Government has to be stopped.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has argued that threats to the national security of Canada are hypothetical and, therefore, we do not require these powers, except to destroy democracy. He is very far out of touch with reality. I cannot imagine many Canadians being fooled, even by his eloquent rhetoric, into believing that this is a Bill which the Government wants to use to destroy the country and to destroy our democracy.
1 want to ask the Hon. Memver a question. He talks about hypothetical threats. He should know that there are real threats to our security. I want to put to him a problem and ask how he would handle it. If we received information, as we sometimes do in Government, which we believed, that KGB members or known terrorists have come to Canada, and we assessed the basis of that belief and came to agree with it, does he think we should have no authority at all to engage in surveillance of them because they are not necessarily committing a crime or that we do not have evidence of that crime? Is he suggesting that there should not be authority, that there are not sensible reasons why their mail, under proper safeguards, should not be investigated? He may not like the safeguards in the Bill. I want to raise with him the proposition that surely even he, as fanatically anti-government as he is, might recog-
February 13, 1984

nize that there are some circumstances in which KGB members or members of other hostile intelligence services may come to this country, and that we would get credible evidence of it, or that international terrorist groups may come here bearing in mind that the Olympics will take place in North America this year, that His Holiness the Pope will be visiting our country this year, that Her Majesty will be here in August, in all of these circumstances-
We have the police.

The Hon. Member reminds me that we have the police. I am not asking whether we should go after them with police methods. 1 know he would agree with that. What I am asking is, if we know about them, is there not justification for having access to their mail and justification for being able to put them under surveillance without knowing whether they intend to engage in particular crimes?
Mr. Speaker, I am somewhat amazed at the question that has been put to me. First of all, it seems to suggest that the present law enforcement agencies are totally inadequate to handle-
That is not what I said.

1 agree there could be very illegitimate threats against Canadian society, against His Holiness the Pope when visiting Canada and the Olympics being held in North America. These could conceivably be targets for foreign terrorists. I quite agree. Is the Minister telling us that at present the RCMP does not have the ability to monitor and take precautions against these foreign threats?
The second point I wish to make is that when the Minister introduced the legislation, I wish had followed the American example more closely and had treated Canadian citizens and landed immigrants somewhat differently from foreign agents. Under this Bill Canadian citizens can be spied upon, their phones tapped, their homes broken into under some pretty, vague definition in this Act, even though there may be no hard evidence that these Canadian citizens are connected with an attempt to assassinate the Pope or carry out some terrorist activity, but are suspect in a vague way, and their basic freedoms denied. 1 wish the Minister would explain the reason for lumping Canadian citizens in with foreign terrorists, KGB, CIA or other agents.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has indeed exposed himself as someone who is unwilling to deal with a very real example. He was asked a question. He is testing the hypothesis. Let me assert again that there are real threats to our national security. We do occasionally get evidence, which we believe, of foreign hostile intelligence officers and members of terrorists groups who come into and through this country. He asks why the police cannot go after them with the normal warrant under the Criminal Code. Under the Criminal Code, as was pointed out, we need to have a reasonable belief of a specific crime or of a criminal plan. In the example I am putting to him, the only evidence we have is that they are here,
Security Intelligence Service
that they happen to be in our country and that they are terrorists. I am asking for his help. I am asking him and Parliament to agree that in circumstances like that, with the kinds of safeguards I am willing to talk about in committee, develop, or change, in that type of environment there should be justification for getting a wiretap without evidence of a specific crime being planned by the particular terrorist group or hostile intelligence officers, that we should be able to open their mail under all the safeguards that this Parliament imposes. Those are simple questions. The Hon. Member avoided them the first time, and I know he will avoid them again.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think the Minister heard my response correctly. First, I admit, and no one in the House would be so foolish as to deny it, that there are potential threats that could occur against Canada from foreign terrorists and foreign intelligence agencies. Given what we have in the world today that is a "given".
The Minister has not answered my question. Why does he include Canadian citizens in the same bunch as foreign terrorists and foreign intelligence agencies? It is one thing to be aware of a foreign terrorist coming into Canada, to intercept his mail and keep tab on his telephone calls. It is quite another thing for a Canadian citizen, who has not broken any law, one who maybe collects money for rebels in El Salvador or Afghanistan, to be considered potentially subversive because that citizen is involved directly in some way in overthrowing a legally constituted government somewhere else. This Bill has lumped all those people together, and I am afraid the Minister has not as yet realized the point we are trying to make.

Mr. Speaker, I guess in the course of this debate I can answer the question, if that will assist the Hon. Member to answer mine. He is asking, why should one consider that Canadians might be capable of acts of terrorism or acts of espionage and subversion? 1 think that just to put that question is to answer it. One likes to have faith in one's countrymen, but we know, our history tells us, that there are Canadians capable of subversive activities, acts of terrorism and espionage. That is the reason the Bill addresses that possibility, and I think he is very naive to deny it. I do not think his constituents or others following this debate will fail to have noticed that he is refusing to address a question which I am asking Parliament to address in dealing with this Bill. I am asking Parliament to recognize circumstances where mail opening and surveillance might be justified without proof or evidence of a crime. He refuses to address that, and that is typical of the NDP.
Mr. Speaker, I will try to be brief, but the Minister's comments require long answers. I thought I had given some of those answers in my remarks.
Come on, yes or no.

We want to make the distinction, as it is made in the United States and most other jurisdictions, between

February 13, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
domestic terrorists and subversives and foreign terrorists and subversives. Part of our criticism of this legislation is that it does not make that distinction. The point we want to make is that the Criminal Code already gives the police ample powers to open the mail of domestic terrorists-
It does not.
-and to listen to their telephone conversations.
It does not.
This Government has over 800,000 files on Canadians, and it tells me it wants more. Surely, Mr. Speaker, enough is enough.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 45, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell)- Fisheries-Future of independent fish companies in Nova Scotia; the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson)- Royal Canadian Mounted Police-McDonald Commission findings of law-breaking-Decision not to take disciplinary action, (b) Request for withdrawal of security service legislation; the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm)- National Revenue-Department's seizure of taxpayers' assets, (b) Taxpayers' costs in appealing assessments.

The House resumed consideration of the Motion of Mr. Kaplan that Bill C-9, an Act to establish the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, to enact an Act respecting enforcement in relation to certain security and related offences and to amend certain acts in consequence thereof or in relation thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words in connection with Bill C-9. I think the proper procedure is to debate this Bill openly and get as much representations as we can from the people of Canada. I think I would be very safe in saying that the people of Canada generally are concerned about having a good intelligence service, one of the best. They
are also concerned about whether it is done through the RCMP or by a new body called the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. Some great nations have had separate services. The United States and England have separate services, and that seems to work out very satisfactorily. I think there are some advantages to having a separate intelligence service, as well as some advantages in having it remain with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. If the people of Canada generally, and this House of Commons in particular, decide to separate the service from the RCMP, I do not think it will be a blot on the RCMP, not at all. We all admire the RCMP; they have done a tremendous job in policing, and they still have a tremendous job to do. But if the decision is made to separate the service, then I think we have to institute safeguards concerning accountability, in order to make sure the intelligence service is checking on spies and fifth column activities, not on the people who have as great a desire as we do to build a great country but who have different ideas on how it should be done.
We have to be very careful in that respect, Mr. Speaker. Canada is a young country compared to the European and Asiatic countries. We are still in the developing stage in many respects. My friend, the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Footh-ills (Mr. Thacker), was speaking this morning about political groups which arise from time to time. Some of them have disappeared, some have made a contribution and then disappeared, and some never got off the ground. But I do not think we should ever stop any group of people in Canada from using the means they think is best to build a great country. All the wisdom is not wrapped up in the Liberal Party, the Conservative Party, the Socialist Party or the Communist Party. People have different ideas and different views. Sometimes they bring a fresh look to problems which arise.
In the early days of Alberta, after the Liberal administration ruled the Province for about ten or 11 years, the people decided not to go to the Conservatives and not to go back to the Liberals, who had made a tremendous dent in the credit of the Province and had had many scandals with the railways, and so on. They went to a brand new Party headed by a lawyer, the late John E. Brownlee, and the Party was known as the United Farmers of Alberta. It was in power until 1935 and it did a lot of good things. It moved the telephone lines so that rural people could have telephones. That is still remembered as one of the big things done by the UFA. It also went to the Canadian Government and begged, pleaded and demanded ownership of our natural resources the same as other provinces. Finally, in 1930 the federal Government gave the province ownership of its natural resources so that we were on a par with the other provinces in Canada. That one item stands out conspicuously in the UFA administration. But what if there had been an intelligence service when that Party was first started and we had said to them, "No, we cannot have this, you are talking a new language"? They were talking a new language, Mr. Speaker. They were going to do things that the old line Parties were not prepared to do at that time. Had
February 13, 1984

they been stopped it would have been a pretty serious thing because they were just as loyal as any of us.
Then there was the Social Credit Government which was formed. That Party was led by the late William Aberhart, a powerful man, and to hear him speak about the banks you would never think he had been a Conservative. He talked about the power of the banks. He saw that the people were hungry but that goods were available, so he thought, why not get the money to distribute the goods to the people so that they would no longer be hungry in the midst of plenty? He had a new theory, but had the intelligence service been in existence it would have thought he was going to turn the country upside down. It would have been a sad thing if his group had not held power, because for the next 35 or 36 years they gave good government and good leadership to Alberta. I think of people like Premier Manning and Premier Aberhart who were strong men, loyal to Canada and who wanted all the people to have a share in the great wealth of the country.
More recently there was the separatist movement in western Canada. Most if not all of those people were loyal Canadians but they had a different idea. They thought that with the heavy populations of Quebec and Ontario, it will never be possible for the Maritimes or the West to get a fair deal. I argued the other way. I say that the salvation of the country can rest in the reform of the Senate where we can have a check and balance on what goes on when an arrogant government is in power. Had we had a check and balance when the National Energy Program was introduced, it would never have gone through, and it would not have ruined the industry in western Canada. Had we had a check and balance when the Crow Bill went through, we would not have had the present tremendous weight on the grain producers of western Canada, giving them a load that they cannot carry with incomes going down and expenses going up.
If we had reform, it would be the salvation of the country. Every region must be treated fairly. However, I would not want the intelligence service to be dealing with a group because its idea of the way to run the country is different from the orthodox view. That is one of the dangers I see in any intelligence service.
We want the intelligence service to do a tremendous job in seeking out fifth columnists, those who are out to destroy the country, who would sell us to another power so that they could gain everything they wanted from the wealth of this great land. That is the fifth column I am dealing with, not Canadians who want to better the country and who have a different idea of how to do it.
Whether we have the RCMP or an intelligence service, Mr. Speaker, there has to be accountability. I do not think we can give free rein to any intelligence service to do what it likes and not be responsible to anyone. That simply would not work. With its quasi military setup, the RCMP has responsibility, right from the Commissioner down. Each detachment has a leader to take the responsibility if a constable, a corporal or an
Security Intelligence Service
officer gets out of line. That is one of the reasons why people in the West strongly favour the intelligence service continuing to rest with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. They know that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is a disciplined group and is accountable. Those in charge at the Royal Canadian Mounted Police should be accountable to the Government of Canada. In turn, the Government of Canada should take responsibility when it gives orders to the RCMP to do things that perhaps it would rather not do. There is no doubt in my mind that orders were given to the RCMP with respect to the fracas in Quebec. Not for one minute could I believe that the RCMP would burn down barns, steal records or break down doors of their own volition. I have too much respect for them to think that. But they do obey orders. If they get an order to do something, they will do it. That is part of their discipline, part of their training, part of their life. It is the same with a soldier, an airman or a sailor in wartime. You cannot have democracy in wartime. You cannot have democracy in the army. You have to be able to take orders and let somebody make the decision. Sometimes the rank and file think the decision is all haywire. Many times in the air force I thought the commanding officer was haywire, but eventually it turned out he knew what he was doing.
I remember taking all the shots preparatory to going to the Far East with the air force. The whole squadron was anxious to go, but suddenly we got word to come back to Canada. I thought the Canadian Government had gone wacky, getting us all prepared then sending us back to Canada. Much as we were glad to come back to Canada, we had volunteered for the Far East. A few days later we found that the bomb had landed and we realized that the Canadian Government knew what it was doing in ordering the troops back to Canada, because the war was practically over.
There must be someone accountable, someone to make the decisions, and we have that in the RCMP. It is one of its strong points. The point I raised with my colleague this morning is the possibility of infiltration by fifth columnists. That is difficult in the RCMP. You do not start at the top in that service, you start at the bottom and work up. If someone has subversive trends, surely that would be found out in five, 10, 15 or 20 years. Such people would not last in the RCMP, and that is one of its strong points. The fifth columnist would have a difficult job to get into the RCMP and influence its intelligence service.
We found that fifth columnists were able to get into the intelligence service in Great Britain and in the United States. They were very clever about it. Perhaps it is possible in the RCMP, but I doubt it. Certainly it would be possible in a separate service, because that has proved to be the case in the U.S.A. and in Great Britain. It is one of the advantages of the RCMP and one of the disadvantages of a separate service.
On the other hand, a separate service could attract highly trained, intelligent people skilled in this particular field. The RCMP are trained as well. I spoke to an officer in Alberta whom I had known when he was just a boy. He had been with the security service and had left it to return to the work of the
1334

February 13, 1984
Security Intelligence Service
detachment because he felt so much consideration was being given to separating the security service that he wanted to be sure he remained an RCMP officer. It had been his life's ambition to be in the RCMP, but he left the security service, although he said that the training he had received in the intelligence service was standing him in good stead.
Many people think that the training in separate universities and in other fields is going to be advantageous in the separate service. Perhaps it will, but time will tell. If we go that route we had better be sure that we take special steps to see to it that fifth columnists, particularly from other countries, do not infiltrate our intelligence service.
What I want to emphasize is accountability. I believe the Government has to be responsible. Whoever the director is, he surely must be responsible to a Minister, and the Minister must be responsible to the House of Commons, and in turn the Members of the House of Commons must be responsible to the people. This is democracy. We should not sidestep democracy in any of our services, whether it be intelligence, revenue or whatever. Democracy will work if there is that line of responsibility from the Minister, who is appointed to the Cabinet and responsible to the House of Commons or to the legislature, and the Members of the House of Commons or the legislature who are responsible to the people. That is the strength of democracy. That should be the paramount objective in developing this service. Are we going to have accountability? We must have accountability and the Minister must take the responsibility. I do not agree at all with former Solicitors General when they say, "I do not take the responsibility for what the RCMP did". The Minister must take the responsibility. I certainly want to emphasize the matter of accountability. When this Bill goes to committee, let us make sure that, whatever route the majority takes with regard to the intelligence service, the director is responsible to the Minister and the Minister is responsible to the House of Commons which, in turn, is responsible to the people. If we go that route, whether it is the RCMP or a separate service, I feel we will have an excellent intelligence service in this country.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions, comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to rise today and speak on Bill C-9. I do not believe I have seen in the four years I have been here a Bill placed before the House which is more complicated and difficult to understand and one which raises so many questions and which affects so many people all across Canada. On my reading through the Bill, through the Senate committee report and through Bill C-157, a number of questions arose which I feel need to be asked. When this Bill goes to committee, I hope that my colleagues will address those questions in a very reasonable way.
We in Canada live in and support the system in which we have the kind of Government we have, with all its imperfections. We feel free to talk about Senate reform and about changing the rules in the House of Commons. Indeed, we prize, I believe above all else, the freedom which individuals have, not only to move freely within the country but to go home and close our doors at night, and, understanding our laws, feel free to discuss Government in any way we wish. One is free to form a Party which is opposed to the present Government, opposed to the way we are doing things. I have always had a sense of pride that we in Canada allow a Communist Party openly to exist in the country. We allow it to espouse all sorts of things about Canada which it has done freely during elections when people can even run on a Communist ticket. That does not happen in all other countries, but our system is such that we allow this freedom because we know the system we have will not be undermined when things are brought out into the open.
I would like to speak about some of the questions I have about this Bill which, hopefully, the committee will address when the Bill goes for a clause by clause study. I refer first to Bill C-157, Clause 14(2). It states, and I quote:
The Service is not restricted from "remaining informed" about the political, economic and social environment within Canada.
The Senate recommendation is not followed in this instance, and it raises the question as to why it was not. The Senate committee report stated, and I quote:
There is nothing to prevent the service from "remaining informed", indeed this is a necessity. To include this section is to "court mischief' as the words are unnecessary.
The Senate says that to include this section is to court mischief. We have seen this type of mischief when we have looked to our neighbour to the south. We have seen the things which happened at Watergate. We have seen the mischief which happened in political campaigns. We have seen mischief in other areas. The Senate committee report is clearly saying to the House of Commons, "If you include the words in there, it could court mischief'. If the Senate committee believes that those words in the Bill are unnecessary, why are they still in the Bill?
In Clause 2, "threats to the security of Canada" are defined
as:
-espionage or sabotage against Canada or "any state allied or associated with Canada" or activities directed toward or in support of such espionage or sabotage.
The Senate committee recommendation, which was not followed, stated that the words "espionage" and "sabotage" are not defined in the Bill. What constitutes espionage? What constitutes sabotage? Do we leave this definition with the Minister of the day? Do we leave this definition to the security service itself? I suggest that the security service, by nature of its business, can see "sabotage" and "espionage" in a variety of areas and in a variety of ways, unless we have a clear definition of what those terms mean. One could water the term down to mean an activity on the stock market which could sabotage the economy. It could mean someone attempting to deal in securities or in Canadian currency in such a way that he moves the price up or down. I believe some lawyers could
February 13, 1984

very easily interpret those words to mean that espionage is heavy speculation in Canadian currency. I believe these words must be clearly defined. We are leaving too much out that I as a layman do not understand and, I am sure, that many people within the law societies and members of the Bar do not understand either. The terms should be defined so that we all know exactly what they mean. Sabotage is already an offence under the Criminal Code and it is defined. My question is, what does the word espionage really mean? The dictionary definition is that it is spying and section 3 of the Official Secrets Act defines it very broadly. I think espionage should be defined in the Bill and I would ask my colleagues to address this problem when it goes to committee.
Clause 2(c) of the previous Bill C-157 referred to activities within or relating to Canada directed toward or in support of the threat or use of acts of violence against persons or property for the purpose of achieving a political objective within Canada or a foreign state. The provincial attorneys general voiced their concern about this definition being far too broad. I agree with them. I do not know all that the Senate was referring to. There were several witnesses who appeared before the Senate committee who urged that a change be considered and that the definition be set up in such a way as to deal only with the threat or use of acts of serious violence. We see people across Canada demonstrating against the Cruise missile testing, for example. In their protest marches they may break through a first line of defence which the Armed Forces have put up around an air base or even around the House of Commons. We see fences put up when people are demonstrating. It seems to me that it is not serious violence if they break through the barriers, and indeed even come into the outer lobby of the House of Commons to voice their opinion. I do not think that would be viewed by any Member in the House as serious violence. It seems to me that we are putting a provision in this Act which could view that action as being against the Act. I think it would be a serious restraint on the freedom of individuals to express themselves in the way in which they have become accustomed. I am not speaking about a saboteur or undercover agent using serious violence by setting into motion a situation where explosives are used to derail a train or something like that. To me that is serious. There are other activities that do not meet this criterion. I ask that my colleagues consider that very carefully in the legislation.
Section 18 deals with international affairs and defence. This allows the service, in relation to Canada's defence or its conduct of international affairs, to assist in Canada with the collection of information or intelligence respecting a foreign state or foreign person. I am not sure whether the service should be engaged in this type of work, as it is not linked to the security of Canada. I think the way it is presently laid out is too broad and should be narrowed down and linked to the security of Canada. The conduct of international affairs, not linked with the security of the nation, should not be included here. That area has to be studied.
Security Intelligence Service
Where are the parameters of this provision? Testimony before the Senate committee specified that this section will be used to gather economic, commercial and social data about other nations. I can understand the need for economic and commercial data and indeed for social data of other nations, particularly nations with which we have entered into foreign aid agreements. We in Canada would be miffed if we found out that the security services of other nations were gathering information in a secretive manner regarding our economy, commerce and society. In most cases in a free society this information is available anyway. I do not understand the necessity for connecting these two together.
Warrants can be issued to allow the service to use intrusive techniques under this section. How does a judge determine whether to issue a warrant? In my mind the security service is there to protect the security of our country, yet we are arming it with the authority to use techniques clearly subversive in another country to gather commercial, economic and other kinds of data which are not related to the security of our country. I can envisage people from the new security agency or senior RCMP officers in the security service posted to our embassies in other countries and being expelled holus bolus because we are arming them with the authority to do subversive work in another country. I am not sure that is what we want to do. Since warrants are issued to enable the service to perform its functions and duties, will a judge always issue a warrant in Canada if the relevant Minister requests the service to act under this provision? He may not. More work has to be done on that section, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to comment on the powers afforded in this Bill. Section 22 gives the service extraordinary powers by warrant. I always worry about extraordinary powers. If a judge is satisfied that the service requires a warrant to perform its duties and functions under the Act, he may issue a warrant which allows the service to intercept any communication or obtain any information, record, document or thing. That is very broad indeed and clearly can be abused. After a great deal of study, the Senate committee suggested that a balance was called for between the gravity of the threat to security and the intrusion into the privacy of those affected by the warrant.
