speechtext:
that Bill C-212, an Act to amend the Interest Act, be read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, once again it is my pleasure to rise and debate this very small Bill which I have introduced. This Bill was debated in the House on March 2, 1983, but it is still very much apropos that it should be debated again at this time.
I hope to draw the attention of the House and Canadians to the plight of hundreds of thousands among us who are trapped into paying excessively high interest rates on their mortgages. I am referring to the dilemma facing Canadian families who are forced to pay 17 per cent, 18 per cent or 21 per cent interest on mortgages which today might be refinanced in the range of 12 per cent.
When I introduced this Bill last year I checked with CMHC and found that there were 700,000 Canadians who had mortgages at 17 per cent or higher. I do not know what the updated figures are as the statistics taken in the 1981 census have not been compiled as yet, according to Statistics Canada. Surely the figure would be approximately 150,000 fewer, but there are still approximately 500,000 Canadians who are faced with these high interest rates.
Bill C-212 suggests a means by which these home-owners might take advantage of today's lower interest rates. Quite simply, it would provide them with a means of paying off their present mortgage with a three-month penalty, thereby allowing them to apply for a new mortgage at a lower rate.
This bill is intended to try to bring the Interest Act of today up to date in harmony with the present practices. Let me briefly explain what the present practice is. Since as far back as 1907, the Interest Act has contained the same Section 10. It may even go back to when the first Interest Act was introduced in what was then Upper Canada of 1859, but it has been around for as long as Canada has existed. That section provides that if a person has a mortgage for a term longer than five years, at the end of five years it could be paid off with a three-month penalty. Of course, it has been the norm in this country for a number of decades to have 25 year mortgages. This means that in one fifth of the term of a 25 year mortgage, people could decide to pay their mortgage off by paying a three-month penalty. That seemed to be fair and worked in this country for at least 60 years, until 1967 and 1968 when the mortgage lending institutions, the trust companies and banks, unilaterally changed that equilibrium that had survived over decades and reduced it to a 10-year mortgage. That is
when inflation began to get out of hand. It was approximately 4 per cent then.
I want to suggest that these institutions have gone further. When interest rates began to get way out of line for the first time in our history, from 1979 to 1983, they further reduced that term to a maximum mortgage of five years, then three years and finally one year. At one point, one could only get a six-month mortgage. In the last year some companies have lengthened the term again to five years. However, as Hudac's John Sandusky stated in an article in the Financial Times of December 5, 1983, "Having access to long term money remains a higher priority for the housebuilders". It is not only a priority for the house builders but it is that also for the house lenders and the people who are borrowing money to buy the houses. The lending institutions changed that 60-year equation of a 25 year mortgage in which it could be paid off after five years. They unilaterally changed it to suit themvelves.
I am suggesting now that we should put this back into a fair equation so that if five years was one fifth of a 25 year mortgage, then after one fifth of the term of any mortgage the mortgagor would be able to pay off the mortgage with a three-month penalty. That is the essence of this Bill. It does not matter whether this Bill is passed or whether Members would sooner discharge it and have the subject matter sent to committee; I want it explored.
I know what the lending institutions will say. They will say that they have borrowed money at 16 per cent and lent it out at 18 per cent and five year GICs and so on. I want to say that if the Government wants to listen to the big lending institutions, with all of their profits and big bucks, and not listen to the little guy, then let it go ahead. But the Government is just giving in to the big banks. I believe it should listen to the little person in this country.
In that respect let me make a few comments about the banks. On October 18, research showed that the spread in the bank rate, between the inflation rate and the bank rate, was the highest it was in 10 years except for once in December, 1980. With respect to the real interest rate, the spread between the chartered rate and the bank rate was the highest in any year and any month in the last 10 years except for the month of December, 1980.
Last fall, the chartered bank prime spread was running at approximately 5.5 per cent to 6 per cent. In 1972 it was running at .90 per cent. In December, 1973, it was .20 per cent. In December, 1976, it was 3.75 per cent. In January, 1983, it was 3.70 per cent. The banks are not hurting right now. But let them come to the committee and give us their tale of woe. I would like to ask them a few questions.
I have here a few examples, of which there are many. The trust companies keep pleading that they are hurting so much. In a Globe and Mail article on December 8, 1983, it states that for the previous year, Financial Trust Company earned 56 cents but for the last nine months up to December, 1983, it has earned 98 cents a share. Victoria and Grey had gone from $1.15 a share in 1982 to $1.79 a share in the same period of time. They are not necessarily hurting either. Let us not listen
February 13, 1984

to their story of woe without giving them a chance to explain all the details.
In a periodic news release of March, 1983, from Gardiner and Watson, a reputable brokerage firm in Canada, they talk about the net interest margins: mortgages versus GICs. In that article they state that as a rule of thumb the spread between mortgages and GICs has been roughly 1.50 per cent so that against current rates, trust companies will improve their spreads by 25 to 125 basis points, depending on the term the new business assumed. They are saying that they are making more money. They had a bigger spread in 1983, when this was written, than they had in previous years. What they are saying is that they are making more money. They have a bigger spread now in 1983 when this was written than they have had in previous years.
I do not want to speak for a very long time but I want to point out a couple of things which should be pertinent to the Government. For example, on June 24, 1974 at 5.45 p.m. EDT, the time for release, we had the following main points: Prime Minister's statement on consumer affairs, which reads in part:
The Liberals will make it a legal right to prepay residential mortgages during the first five years of the mortgage agreement, if the person wishes to do so, without excessive penalties. The law in general permits prepayment after five years-
That was a promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and embellished a little bit in one of the news reports. I do not have the exact words of what he said. I just have the text released from his office that he was going to reduce the right to prepay with a three-month penalty. That is what was promised by the Liberals in 1974. Why have the Liberals not lived up to the promise? I say to the Liberals, "Do not listen to the banks and the trust companies. Bring in a Bill. Let us have the subject examined at length, especially in light of the record high interest rates and the penalties that some of the financial institutions want of $6,000, $7,000, $8,000, $9,000 and $12,000. What is the matter? Bring it in and let us take a look from the consumers' point of view.
I want to bring up a matter which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) mentioned on March 28, 1983 in the House of Commons in reply to a question. In 1983 after this Bill had been introduced, the Minister said:
Indeed, Madam Speaker, the point raised by the Hon. Member seems very worthwhile to me, and a three-month penalty would seem reasonable to me under the circumstances. In addition, I would suggest that, if there are other cases such as those mentioned by the Hon. Member, they should be brought to my attention, and I undertake to have them submitted to the institutions involved, either by the Inspector General of Banks or any other appropriate agency, so that they will be closely scrutinized, in an effort to prevent financial institutions from being unfair to some citizens.
The Minister of Finance was on the side of the Prime Minister. Then, of course, on October 11, 1983 the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) spoke to reporters. The CP report read:
The act already gives buyers that option-but only after a mortgage has been in force at least five years. Both NDP and Progressive Conservative MPs have
Interest Act
been pressing the Liberals for months to make the law less restrictive. The Government's main response so far has been to use moral suasion on banks and trust companies.
It has failed. The CP story continued with, "but certainly we feel we must take some kind of action, Erola said Tuesday". Home buyers by the thousands took out or renewed mortgages when rates were 18 per cent or higher. "In fact, in many cases prepayment penalties as high as ten months have been brought to my attention, Erola said". I can bring them to her attention for three years. The Minister refused to say when the Government will decide for sure whether to bring in a Bill on behalf of home owners. This is a Bill on behalf of home owners, not on behalf of the banks and trust companies. However, the banks did say that any changes in the law would not be retroactive. That is fine. At least bring in changes to make things a little fairer and balance out that equation which for 60 years was there until it was upset by the lending institutions.
There were a number of other discussions, and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs talked very positively and said that the Bill would be out very soon. But it never happened. We are still waiting and we are hoping that it is not too late. It is very timely that this discussion is going on before the Budget which will be delivered on Wednesday afternoon. Perhpas there could be last minute changes yet. We hope so.

I noticed that on October 13, 1983 even the Hon. Member for Oshawa, the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), finally got in on the act about discussing interest rates on mortgages.
On investigation in the United States we find it is very normal for people to get away with a three-month penalty. In one large pool of funds which is quasi government controlled with $149 billion in the pot people in 29 States can get away with paying off at any time what is a 30-year mortgage to start with at one year, three years, five years, by paying a three-month penalty. In other States, there is no penalty at all. The thrust of paying off a mortgage with a three-month penalty is the same as that which people have in the United Kingdom. It people in the U.K. and people in the U.S. can do that, why can we not do it in Canada?
I have spoken about Victoria and Grey, the trust company. I hope no one will say, "The poor trust company is not doing that well." Now I read in the papers that the Victoria and Grey is going to start a bank of its own. I worry about the Royal Trust. It has had the Royal Trust Bank in Florida for a number of years, which it is trying to sell off. It is not sold as yet, I understand. But through that facility the Royal Trust has been able to lend money under the terms necessary in the U.S.
If it is good enough in the United States, and all Canadians believe that we should be doing what is done in the U.S.,

February 13, 1984
Interest Act
where a person can get out of a 30-year mortgage in 39 States with a three month penalty and with no penalty in the others, why not here?
This matter should go to committee at least. We should have an inquiry. I would be quite happy to have this Bill discharged and have the subject matter referred to a committee, if anyone wants to suggest it. I think we should have the courage to stand up for the consumers, the people, and not the financial institutions. I am not saying financial institutions do not have a right to come and explain their position. Maybe they will persuade me and the rest of us differently. But let them come and explain in an open committee, not just in the back rooms of the Minister of Finance's suite. I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary will have a chance to expound on this in a few moments. 1 say, let us give the people a break. There are at least 500,000 who are trapped. Let us follow what the Minister of Finance asked in 1981 when he asked for the financial institutions to bleed a little. They have all had increased profits. They have never bled. There were more foreclosures in 1983 than in 1982. There will probably be more in 1984 than in 1983. People lasted for a period of time, but with the length of the recession they have run out of all their reserves and they will still lose their homes. I hope the Government will allow the subject matter, if not the Bill, to go to committee.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   INTEREST ACT AMENDMENT RESPECTING MORTGAGE PAY-OUTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say it is a pleasure to be able to say a few words regarding Bill C-212, introduced by the Hon. Member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick). I believe he is on the right track in suggesting that perhaps we ought to amend the Interest Act and get on with doing something for the people of Canada as opposed to the financial institutions. I do not want to suggest for a moment that we ought to go out and bad mouth the banks, the trust and loan companies, the credit unions or the caisses. The banks of Canada have existed in an atmosphere or environment of privilege for many years. When we look at the return on equity of the major banks of Canada, year after year we notice that it averages in excess of 16 per cent. 1 do not believe there is another sector of our economy or another business in the country which would say that over the last number of decades its return on equity has been in the 16 per cent range on average. In plain English this means that the banks are doing better than virtually any other sector of the economy. One could make a case for a couple of areas where there have been some improvements or perhaps challenges to the banks. I am referring to those areas in which the Government regulates the prices, such as utilities, pipelines and the like. However, by and large I do not think there is a single Canadian, if he or she were to be honest, who would not say that the Canadian banking establishment operates in a privileged environment.
This Bill is asking why we should not have in Canada the same situation which exists in other lands where people, through their governments, have indicated, particularly during
these difficult times, that they want to pay off their mortgages-and I suspect this is something every Canadian family would like to do if it were able-and are not penalized for making this very prudent decision. At the moment countless examples have been brought to the attention of Members of Parliament of people interested in paying off their home mortgages but because of the incredible penalties assessed these individuals, they found that it was not in their interests to do it or that they could not do it.
I remember very distinctly a few months ago when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) rose in his place day after day and told the people of Canada that they need not fear these penalties. He felt that a three-month penalty clause was adequate. He wanted to know about anyone who was charging more. He wanted the evidence on his desk because he was going to take action and bring it to the attention of the appropriate financial institution or of the Inspector General of Banks. I suspect that gave a signal to Canadians that the Minister meant that in his position of responsibility and authority he would do something about anything over a three-month penalty. 1 suspect I personally received 200 or 300 letters from people in my constituency who were caught in that situation. They indicated that they had heard the Minister of Finance on national television or had read in the newspaper and that they took him at his word. They wrote, "Here is my mortgage, here is what I am prepared to do, and here is what the mortgage company said it was not prepared to accept". He asked them to bring it to his attention, so they did that, only to find that in every instance nothing was done. In other words, the Minsiter of Finance inadvertently mislead many people when he suggested that a three-month penalty clause was appropriate.
Essentially, Bill C-12 takes the Minister at his word. It says to the Minister of Finance and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), "You have said this is appropriate, so let us refer it to the Finance Committee for some discussion".

The Hon. Member opposite, who used to chair the Finance Committee, says that this has been discussed. It might have been discussed years ago, but the problem is now. Now is when we are in the depths of a recession; in some parts of the country we are in the depths of a depression. Now is when people need some relief.
Just a few months ago the Prime Minister said that the banks should be bleeding along with everyone else. There is no blood on the steps of the banking institutions of this country. The mortgage holders of Canada want a fair deal such as they would receive if they were residents of other countries. The Minister of Finance has promised them that.
February 13, 1984

We ask the Government to give us the opportunity to discuss this issue in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. We are not asking it to make any commitments today, but certainly it is a topic which touches the lives of thousands of Canadians. Also we ask for representatives of the financial institutions to appear before the committee and make their case and for various consumer groups to appear before it and make their case. Then we can let the committee decide. 1 have faith that Hon. Members on the Finance Committee will weight the evidence carefully and, based upon that evidence, will make a recommendation to the Minister of Finance or not, depending on the case which could be made.
We are not asking for the Government to take a definitive position today. We are not asking for a final answer or a final decision. We are simply asking for a reference or a referral to the obvious committee so that we can deal effectively with an amendment to the Income Tax Act. I suspect that the importance of this particular Bill would ensure that it received a quick hearing and that it will be dealt with expeditiously by Hon. Members. I do not see any reason that we ought to be hesitant in referring this, rather than talking about and letting another good suggestion die in Parliament before it is referred and receives adequate consideration and study.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   INTEREST ACT AMENDMENT RESPECTING MORTGAGE PAY-OUTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when preparing for the debate this afternoon, I fully intended to congratulate the Hon. Member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) on raising this issue in the House. However, after listening to the Hon. Member, I am afraid I had to change my mind, because what he said was really not on target, and not once but several times.
First of all, he would have us believe that only he and his Party are concerned about the problems of home owners. That is just not true, and I may refer the Hon. Member to a passage in the last Throne Speech where the Government announced it would be proposing legislation to further strengthen confidence in the housing market by giving greater protection to home owners and by broadening the choice of mortgage instruments. These measures should increase the accessibility and security of home ownership, provide a greater measure of confidence and stability to the homebuilding industry, and enhance the flexibility of the mortgage market.

Second, the simplistic solution of the Hon. Member is clearly not the answer. He has not really put forward any changes or any new ideas since the last time his Bill was debated in the House in the previous session of this Parliament. Indeed, many know that the current three-month penalty on a five-year mortgage is said to have caused disappearance of the long-term mortgage, that is those over five years. He had nothing to say about that particular problem.
As the Hon. Member should know, financial institutions operate on the basis of the difference between lending rates
Interest Act
and savings rates. By introducing uncertainty on the lending side, everyone knows that the same would be done on the savings side. This could have negative consequences for depositors-consumers, widows and pensioners.

Third, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member grossly oversimplified an issue that is very complex. He referred to a statement made by the Prime Minister in 1974, namely, that the Government intended to propose amendments or legislation that would enable mortgage holders to prepay their mortgages. The Hon. Member has been sitting in the House for ten years, and I wonder where he really was all this time. Was he wide awake when the subject was being debated in the House and in the Committees of the House? If he was, he should be aware that a Bill was tabled at the time by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
Indeed the Borrowers' and Depositors' Protection Act, which was introduced on October 27, 1976, in response to the promise of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), would have allowed a borrower to prepay the full amount of a mortgage loan after three years upon paying a penalty of three months' interest. These proposals received much criticism, probably from the Hon. Member and his Party-

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   INTEREST ACT AMENDMENT RESPECTING MORTGAGE PAY-OUTS

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   INTEREST ACT AMENDMENT RESPECTING MORTGAGE PAY-OUTS
speechtext:
I was not here in 1976. The Hon. Member was, so I will let him answer the question. These proposals received much criticism on the grounds that they would result in all borrowers paying higher interest rates to compensate lenders for losses incurred due to prepayment when rates decline. This is the problem I referred to in my earlier comments. They would make matching of funds more difficult. They would have reduced the volume of mortgage funds available and would have reduced the variety of mortgage vehicles available to borrowers.
With the demise of this piece of legislation and the end of attempts to implement comprehensive consumer credit legislation at the federal level, the thrust turned to join federal-provincial co-operation for reform. It was hoped to achieve uniform and adequate credit regulations through a series of changes to existing federal and provincial statutes, including at the federal level the Interest Act and the Bank Act.
The federal-provincial task force on consumer credit, which was created in 1977, was instructed to develop suitable reform measures. After lengthy discussions, the task force was able, in 1980, to agree upon a mortgage prepayment formula which would have allowed prepayment in full at any time and would have limited prepayment penalties to three months' interest. However, this scheme, when put to federal and provincial Ministers of Consumer Affairs at the conference of October, 1980 was not unanimously accepted, and the task force was instructed to examine the matter of mortgage prepayment

February 13, 1984
Interest Act
further. I wonder if the Elon. Member has ever taken the trouble to refer to the deliberations of this task force and to the difficulties that have been encountered in coming up with answers to this problem.
The task force was unable to agree on any scheme for regulating mortgage prepayment at subsequent meetings. However, the task force did agree that full disclosure of the terms and conditions of mortgage contracts, including prepayment rights or the lack thereof, should be made to borrowers before they entered agreements. I would like the Hon. Member to know that this proposal has been adopted in the new regulations on cost of borrowing disclosure under the Bank Act, which was put forward by this Government in the last session of Parliament. It contains prescribed forms providing for the disclosure of prepayment terms and conditions. I regret to say that comparable provincial legislation, applicable to all provincially-regulated lenders, has not been forthcoming.
1 would be remiss if I did not mention the assistance provided by this Government under the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan. As we all know, during the period of high interest rates the federal Government and some provincial governments provided assistance to many individuals faced with mortgage renewal. Some provinces subsidized renewed mortgages so that borrowers in difficulty paid effective rates of 12 per cent. The federal Government created the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan, but we did not hear any reference to this in the Hon. Member's comments.
This is a complex question. It not only relates to the matter of prepayment of mortgages, but to the question of full disclosure of information at the time the loans are made. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) conducted a study in the past year of these alleged misrepresentations relating to mortgage negotiations. As we all know, allegations were made about representations by mortgage lenders regarding prepayment penalties. When we had the high interest rates in 1982, certain persons alleged that they were induced to take out a five-year mortgage rather than one of a shorter term. They were allegedly told that they could renegotiate at a lower rate should interest rates decline, provided that a three-month penalty was paid. A study has been conducted by the Marketing Practices Branch of the Bureau of Competition Policy, and the Minister, who has had the benefit of this study, will be making proposals for legislative changes dealing with all aspects of this problem.
In conclusion I refer again to the commitment that was made by this Government in the Speech from the Throne. I assure the Hon. Member and all Canadians that the Government will be bringing forward comprehensive proposals within a short period of time.

This is the second time he has raised this issue. In each case we have seen the strong sense of populism. I suspect, and I am sure other Hon. Members do, that this will lead to his getting kicked out of this Party. I do not know why they would listen to somebody who wants to represent the ordinary man. I warn him that the Tory Party has been throwing out some members and has been stabbing them in the back. That happened in my city with the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blen-karn). He was almost attacked on his nomination. I hope a good, populist, sensitive, conscientious Hon. Member like this one has his nomination all ready, because his Party will come after him for presenting an issue of this sensitivity, particularly one with such a common-sense basis.
In his Bill the Hon. Member has not addressed some important economic facts, which I just want to remind him of. I know the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Evans) will recount in a few minutes some of the history of the efforts made by the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs along this line, but I just want to take a look at the mortgage market as it is today because I think there are some really interesting things happening. In my opinion, the short-term mortgage market-and I am going to come back to this-is a really exciting thing for home owners today. We have one year mortgages down around 10 per cent, and that is pretty good for most home owners. In fact, when you contrast it, as the Hon. Member rightly has, with mortgage rates of a couple of years ago, this is a lot of relief from the 20 per cent level people were once experiencing.
Interest rates, Mr. Speaker, clearly reflect the state of the economy. Today's lower interest rates reflect the great health that we are starting to experience once again in our economy.
February 13, 1984

Interest rates are a symptom. They are not the actual cause of much of our economic disorder; they are a symptom of a deeper disorder. Today's low interest rates are a symptom of underlying health. That is what is important for us to recognize. We have an economy on the road to recovery, an economy that once again is feeling strength, and that is reflected in lower interest rates right across the board. All of us would like to see them lower, and as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has said repeatedly in the House, that is his ambition as well. But we cannot get them lower at the moment because of American interest rates and the influence of that enormous economy south of the border. When their interest rates are as high as they are today, we too must keep ours a little bit higher than we would like. We cannot afford to go too much below the level of their rates or we would have an enormous run on our dollar and we would be once again inviting some weaknesses into our economy. We know, because we are practical people, that our economy cannot get so far out of line with the U.S. While American money markets and interest rates are high, ours must remain at a higher than desirable level as well.
Having said that, I say that 10 per cent is better than 20 per cent and it is good to see it back in the area of 10 per cent again. In fact, I think there are mortgages now which are as good as those offered in 1972. We have to go back all that way before we find some in the same range as they are today. 1 would like to check that but I know we have a kind of health in our economy that we have not seen in a long time. We have the promise of stability in our economy and those things have helped to lower interest rates.
I said at the beginning that I am a person who likes short-term interest rates. I believe that many people last year and two years ago were frightened by the economy and searched for some kind of personal security for their families. They felt that although 18 per cent was not good, it was better than 25 per cent, and they were worried that they were going to be facing 25 per cent mortgages. Consequently, they took five-year mortgages. They thought stability was preferable. They went the long course. They chose the option of predictable interest rates at 18 per cent. That certainly happened in my riding. I have street after street where people have taken out five-year mortgages at very high levels and they look around now at the 10 per cent range and they feel the pain. The Hon. Member's comments on that are very appropriate indeed.
When looking at current rates, Mr. Speaker, some people feel they have been cheated. But we must remember when people draw that comparison, that they signed the papers themselves. In my riding the people who signed those contracts knew what they were doing. They did it for a purpose, a reason. They sought stability. They were frightened by what they saw in the economy and did not want to get into a situation that would be even worse a year down the road. Therefore they gambled and went for five years. I think they knew what they were doing.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-MCDONALD COMMISSION FINDINGS OF LAWBREAKING-DECISION NOT TO TAKE DISCIPLINARY ACTION. (B) REQUEST FOR WITHDRAWAL OF SECURITY SERVICE LEGISLATION
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-MCDONALD COMMISSION FINDINGS OF LAWBREAKING-DECISION NOT TO TAKE DISCIPLINARY ACTION. (B) REQUEST FOR WITHDRAWAL OF SECURITY SERVICE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this point to follow up on a question I asked of the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) in this House on January 31. It concerns the findings of the McDonald Commission with respect to wrongdoing and illegalities on the part of some members of the RCMP security service. At that time I asked the Solicitor General what action he intended to recommend to the Commissioner of the RCMP in so far as disciplinary action is concerned in order to ensure that the rule of law is upheld in this country.
As background to the question I would like to note that the McDonald Commission, following an extensive series of hearings, found a common thread, if you will, running through the actions of the security service, particularly at the senior level. What was found, and I quote from their report; was:
-a willingness on the part of members of the RCMP to deceive those outside the force who have some sort of constitutional authority or jurisdiction over them or their activities.
I should note, Mr. Speaker, that had responsible Ministers, that is, the Solicitors General of the day, been more vigilant and more diligent in pursuing their responsibilities for oversight of the activities of the security service, then certainly it would not have been able to operate in the policy vacuum in which it so obviously operated. I should note, as well, that in a number of cases it was clearly the situation that members of the security service were urged on, at best, wilfully blind to the legality of its operation, by a Cabinet and by Solicitors General who were anxious that they be a little more effective than perhaps they had proven to be during the October 1970 crisis.
It is important in looking at the question of the rule of law and discipline to examine the kinds of activities which were carried out by some members of the security service, the so-called "disruptive measures" and countering measures. For example, a number of measures involved criminal conduct; burning a barn, attempting to render a vehicle inoperative, filing false income tax returns, theft, threats by phone and kidnapping, as well as a number of other activities which, as the McDonald Commission indicated, while not perhaps unlawful, certainly were highly improper and unacceptable. For example, the issuing of false communiques with the intention that the news media and the FLQ sympathizers would regard it as a legitimate call to arms, actually persuading an employer to fire a person suspected of belonging to a subversive group, spreading false information and attempting to disrupt meetings of radical labour organizations by conspicuous surveillance. As the McDonald Commission noted:
These methods violated the rule of law, inflicted damage on Canadian citizens and involved secret attempts to manipulate political events and the news media.
One would have thought, Mr. Speaker, given a history of very serious wrongdoing and criminal illegalities such as that reported by the McDonald Commission, that the Commissioner of the RCMP would have taken at least some disciplinary action, and most importantly, the Solicitor General, ultimately

February 13, 1984
Adjournment Debate
responsible to Parliament for the activities of the RCMP, would have ensured that any disciplinary action which was taken was in fact reported to the public.
In August of last year the Minister of Justice (Mr. Mac-Guigan) stated that the Government did not in fact intend to take any disciplinary action. He said, " ... I recognize it as a responsibility of the Commissioner to proceed in this area", although obviously the Minister cannot wash his hands of his own responsibility. The Minister of Justice said that the Commissioner had decided that it would not be appropriate to institute disciplinary proceedings in any of the instances referred to by the Commission while it remains possible that disciplinary action might result from the findings of Quebec courts.
Subsequent to that statement, it has been suggested by the Solicitor General that, yes, in fact there was disciplinary action but he is not going to tell us when that disciplinary action took place or against whom it took place, or the nature of the disciplinary action. We just have to trust him that somehow in fact this was the case. That is an astonishing statement, surely, for the Solicitor General to make. It is an astonishing statement that we in Parliament, and members of the public, are not entitled to know clearly what disciplinary action, if any, has been taken against those members of the security service who were found to have either broken the law or breached the high standards of ethics which they were obliged to uphold.
I would welcome a clarification from the Solicitor General at this point as to exactly which members of the security service have in fact been disciplined and, if he indicates there has been discipline, what the nature of that discipline was and when that discipline took place. Failing that, Mr. Speaker, surely the rule of law itself is being cast into very serious doubt in this country. How can it be suggested that when discipline does take place it is not in the interest of the Canadian public to know precisely what in fact has been meted out in that regard? This is equally important in terms of other members of the security service who must be put on notice that should similar conduct be repeated in the future we are prepared to take this kind of disciplinary action in these circumstances.
Anything other than a full accounting to the Canadian public in these circumstances amounts to a dereliction of the duty of the Solicitor General in terms of his reporting responsibilities to the people of this country, and also in terms of his responsibility to ultimately oversee the activities of the security service and ensure that it obeys the law and adheres to the high standards which any security service in a democratic societyy must adhere to.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) takes great delight in reminding and re-reminding the Canadian people of what is perhaps the most regrettable chapter in the history of the RCMP. It is certainly the most regrettable in the history of the security service of the RCMP. It is a chapter
which the force, the security service and the Government are working very hard to close and put satisfactorily behind us.
He indicates that disciplinary action would be a proper way of showing respect for the rule of law. I would like to remind Hon. Members that the incidents to which the McDonald Commission referred which dealt with rule of law issues, that is with possible law breaking, were not matters to be looked at by the Commissioner in terms of discipline. They were matters which were to be referred outside of this Ministry and beyond the responsibility of the Commissioner, to federal and provincial attorneys general to make decisions to satisfy the Canadian people with respect to the honouring of the rule of law. I am not the proper Minister and this is not the only Government that should be addressing that question. That is a matter he should address to other Ministers and other Governments if he is not satisfied with the requirements of the rule of law on matters found by the McDonald Commission.
As far as the matter of discipline is concerned, I refer him to the RCMP statute which provides clearly that discipline is a matter within the responsibility and purview of the Commissioner. I informed the House that the Commissioner had addressed that, taken action and reported to me that discipline had been imposed in some cases. If the Commissioner had wanted publicity to be part of the penalty imposed that would have been part of his decision. Our tradition, which I intend to continue to respect, calls for those actions to be within the responsibility in all ways of the Commissioner.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-MCDONALD COMMISSION FINDINGS OF LAWBREAKING-DECISION NOT TO TAKE DISCIPLINARY ACTION. (B) REQUEST FOR WITHDRAWAL OF SECURITY SERVICE LEGISLATION
speechtext: I would like to remind the Hon. Member that we have an opportunity to take a real step to do something to provide for greater accountability and responsibility. That is to take the security service as has been recommended now by two royal commissions and the Senate Committee and re-establish it within a proper system of safeguards and controls where there is independent outside scrutiny and review. I am not asking the Hon. Member to trust me, as he incorrectly quoted me as saying. I am asking him to work with me to help develop our national security on a proper basis in a legislated framework with proper control and review which we can be proud of, which the security service will be much better served by having, and which will better serve the national security of our country. We have had two days of debate now. I look forward soon, with his support, to seeing the matter referred to a parliamentary committee.

subtopic: FISHERIES-FUTURE OF INDEPENDENT FISH COMPANIES IN NOVA SCOTIA
FISHERIES-FUTURE OF INDEPENDENT FISH COMPANIES IN NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure you are well aware of my concerns about the fishery on the East Coast. I rise tonight to reinforce the reason for the question I asked the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans on February 7, and also to show my disappointment at his response. He said that he would take note of my representations. This sometimes means that that is exactly where it ends.
February 13, 1984

My question related to the fact that the Government had guaranteed to pay the Bank of Nova Scotia approximately $70 million over the next five to ten years, and that not all of the money allocated under Bill C-170 for the restructuring of the East Coast fisheries was spent. 1 estimate that to be approximately $45 million. In light of those facts, I asked the Minister to reconsider the small independents on the East Coast who are suffering.
I was not one of those who supported the restructuring Bill, because I have always believed that while restructuring is necessary, the banks should have put the companies on the East Coast that were in difficulty into bankruptcy, rather than the federal Government guaranteeing the bank its loans for the restructured company debts over the next number of years.
There has been no guarantee for the small independents at the federal level. In Nova Scotia, there has been no guarantee for the small independents. In Newfoundland, at least we saw the provincial Government bring in a $12 million loan guarantee to the small independents that might be suffering in order to adopt the restructuring plan. Large companies were also squeezing those independents.
Those small independents are the backbone of every small community, not only in South West Nova but throughout the maritime provinces. Those companies have not come looking for assistance, as the big companies have done, yet they have been hurting. The banks have been squeezing their financing in order to make it difficult for them.
1 am asking that the $45 million that was not spent but allocated for restructuring on the East Coast now be directed toward loan guarantees to the many small independents across the province. The federal Government and both provinces have not only gone ahead to help refinance the off-shore sector, they have also guaranteed off-shore resources for the next five years for this off-shore operation. They have added to their quotas. They have given them red fish in the gulf and access to more northern cod. At the same time, in areas such as south western Nova Scotia where the industry has been able to sell the fish and keep inventories low, the banks have put the squeeze on because of other financial restraints in the off-shore sector. For instance, instead of increasing the allocation in cod, it has been decreased. This was done without even studying the cod stocks that were there. There was a limit set in 1981 and that limit has been maintained. The Minister has promised to do a study but has not done so. During all this time, we have seen this need in the off-shore fishery. I do not believe that they will not be back for more next year.
What I am specifically asking is that assistance be given to the small independents, the inshore fishery in the Maritime Provinces. The Minister has that money now, the $45 million. He does not have to wait for the new fiscal year on April 1 to act on the call for an additional $100 million guarantee. The Minister could be helping those companies immediately.
The fishing season is starting. Our plants are not working. Their finances are spread out. They are looking both to
Adjournment Debate
provincial Governments and the federal Government for some financial guarantees, similar to what was given in the offshore; perhaps not to the extent of the financial commitment the federal Government has made to the offshore sector. The federal Government and the Provinces have made those commitments, asking for guarantees of resources, paying off their debts, without asking them to slim down their operations. Those companies will have more fish to put into inventories next year than they had last year.
There has been no consideration given to the dependency throughout the East Coast on the small independent processors. Unless something is done many plants will not be able to reopen because they cannot get the financing from the lending institutions which they have dealt with in the past. Perhaps pressure has to be put on the banks. Perhaps the banks have not been asked by the Provinces or the federal Government what they are doing to the small independents. If the future on the East Coast is in the fishery, a natural resource, surely Governments at all levels, have to take into account the plight of the many small independents and the inshore fishermen in areas such as those I represent.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: FISHERIES-FUTURE OF INDEPENDENT FISH COMPANIES IN NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to expand in more detail than was possible by the Minister during Question Period last week in response to a question raised by the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell).
Let me say at the outset that the cause taken up by the Hon. Member for South West Nova, that is the plight, and the future stability of the small independent processors, is in my view most legitimate, and one which the Department of Fisheries and Oceans shares with her. We too are very concerned about the small independent processors on Canada's East Coast and across this country. We note and we congratulate those who have survived with no government assistance over the last two or three years. We found it necessary-not as a desirable act, not as something we want to do because there is a list of 100 things in which we would like to be involved, in order to maintain the social and economic base of eastern Canada-to step in and to restructure those large companies.
Having said that, I would like to reiterate at the outset that the primary purpose of the Atlantic Fisheries Restructuring Act, Bill C-170, to which the Hon. Member referred, has been to rejuvenate those major offshore companies which have been or are in the process of being restructured. I would remind the Hon. Member, and all Hon. Members, that there are programs within the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion which are available to all industries, including small fish processing industries, for such things as modernization, expansion and restructuring. All Members are aware that these programs have been used in the past by small independent processors.
Perhaps I would be wise to say that some $45 million remains in a fund and is available. All we have to do is spend it. I recall, Mr. Speaker, as I know you do, just last week seeing a delegation of 114 fishermen from western Canada,

February 13, 1984
Adjournment Debate
and know that as a result of that visit many questions were asked in this House of the Minister about the problems confronting fishermen on the West Coast. I think we have a responsibility as well to address those concerns.
I can say to this House and to all Members that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. De Bane) and his colleagues in cabinet are concerned about the problems confronting small independent processors. A number of possible solutions are currently being examined. I do not know whether having Governments take an equity share position, as was the case in the offshore, is the right solution for what is often a small independent family-owned operation. I can tell you that we recognize that these people have survived when larger companies have not. We recognize that they are still in operation because of their resilience and their entrepreneurial spirit. We recognize as well that that kind of success deserves the attention of the people of Canada and deserves the reward when the need is there. The people of Canada cannot-

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-DEPARTMENT'S SEIZURE OF TAXPAYERS' ASSETS. (B) TAXPAYERS' COSTS IN APPEALING ASSESSMENTS
NATIONAL REVENUE-DEPARTMENT'S SEIZURE OF TAXPAYERS' ASSETS. (B) TAXPAYERS' COSTS IN APPEALING ASSESSMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has become increasingly obvious that individual Canadians are currently experiencing two systems of justice. First, there is justice for the ordinary citizen and, second, justice for the Government. In fact, what we are witnessing is the enactment of a discriminatory double standard in taxation and the means of collecting the money from prosecutions. This will come as no surprise to anyone who has had the misfortune of opposing government rules and regulations in the courts. The struggle against this monolithic state generally leads to a very lengthy legal battle accompanied by considerable costs. Justice in this case, it is very evident, is far more expensive for the private citizen relying on his or her own finances than it is for the Government whose case is fully supported by taxpayers' dollars.
For instance, an appeal launched against the Government can result in excessive costs with virtually no guarantee of success. A crucial decision must be made by a private citizen to appeal a case, whereas the Government with its vast sources of revenue automatically chooses this course of action. I am personally aware of an individual who to date has spent $5,000 on legal fees and estimates the cost of an appeal to be approximately $18,500.
On February 9, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) referring to myself stated:
Should he have specific cases to bring to my attention, I can give him every assurance that we will look into the particular circumstances-
Well, there is the Ernest Herbst Food Company of Downs-view, Ontario. It was found guilty of selling candy bars with a declared weight by ounces only. I was informed by Mr. Herbst that his legal fees thus far have amounted to approximately $5,000 and that he can expect to spend an additional $18,500
for an appeal. His choice, therefore, is to risk an expensive appeal or resign himself to paying the $4,000 fine.
It is appropriate to compare this example with the case of Mr. Jack Halpert and Mr. Ray Christiansen, two independent gasoline retailers who were found innocent by an Ontario Provincial Court judge. Following this decision, the federal Government had no hesitation whatsoever in launching an immediate appeal, using taxpayers' dollars. Not only did it launch the appeal, but it withheld compliance with the court decision to pay both Mr. Halpert and Mr. Christiansen $42,000 in costs. This means that these two small independent dealers are out their costs until the appeals are finalized.
I maintain that Ernest Herbst Food Company in Downsview should be afforded the same opportunity as the Government in its right to appeal. If the Government can use taxpayers' money in court while it appeals its own lost cases, why cannot a private individual who wins a case which the Government has brought to court be entitled to the same opportunity?
What is happening in the tax Department today is that a man is proven or found to be guilty by tax assessors without any day in court. What is happening in reality-and I think every Member of Parliament knows it-is that the taxman comes along and says that a person is being reassessed $200, $800 or even $1,000 more in tax. Individuals say that the new assessments are wrong. We hear people say that a wrong interpretation of the tax law is being made. The bureaucrats say that if the individual believes that then as a taxpayer he has the right of appeal. Then the taxpayer looks at the cost of appealing which could amount to $5,000 or even $50,000- and in the specific case to which I referred, it would be $18,500-and it is more than the amount of the reassessment.
It is a normal human reaction to say "I know I am right as a taxpayer. I would like to prove that I am right. I would like to prove that the taxman is wrong, but it will cost me so much money that I will be better off simply to accept the judgment of the civil servant, the servant of the people." The Minister responded to me on February 9, by saying there is an option open to that individual. That individual can appoint a third party who will guarantee the amounts of the moneys owed to the Government in tax and then we will go ahead and hear the appeal.
I say with all due respect to the Minister that it is one thing for him to say that that person who has been assessed has the right of appointing a third party. It is an entirely different thing to assume that that individual who has been assessed and taxed on business and then driven out of business because of his inability to pay is able to find such a third party to guarantee all the costs, all the fines and the ensuing costs that go with going into receivership, which is very often the case. Often the efforts of the tax people force independent businessmen right out of business today.
If the Minister was fair with the people of Canada he would recognize the need today for some form of financial assistance so that the Halperts and the Christiansen's of Toronto, who
February 13, 1984

have won the cases brought against them by the Government, would be afforded those dollars awarded to them by the court rather than having to wait for perhaps three appeals. Halpert and Christiansen will now have to go to the Ontario County Court, then to the Ontario Court of Appeal and then to the Supreme Court of Canada. In the meantime, the Government is forcing people out of business by its unwillingness to see the other side, and through its heavy-handed approach in the matter of collecting debts to government, without the same opportunities of recourse being available to the independent businessman or the private individual.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-DEPARTMENT'S SEIZURE OF TAXPAYERS' ASSETS. (B) TAXPAYERS' COSTS IN APPEALING ASSESSMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the Hon. Member regarding question he asked on February 9, 1984 dealing with tax problems, one has to ask if it is a responsible act for a member to stand in this House and make charges filled with loaded words and phrases against the department and the Government in general without citing any proof and in disregard of the facts. Take for instance the words and phrases in his question when he originally raised it. First, he claimed that Revenue Canada considers a person guilty without trial; second, locks up businesses without trial and, third, that the Minister justifies the principle of guilty until proven innocent.
The Hon. Member then went on to talk about seizing the bank accounts of children, senior citizens and the handicapped.
Adjournment Debate
He knows, I am sure, that the seizure of a child's bank account was in fact as a result of a mistaken indentity by a bank, not by the Department of National Revenue.
Who are these seniors and handicapped whose accounts have been seized. Has the Hon. Member identified any cases of injustice and has he taken the trouble to inform the Minister about them? Any seizure of bank accounts or garnishee of salaries takes place after a number of other collection steps have failed and after the taxpayer has failed to avail himself or herself of the standing offer to negotiate suitable terms for payment.
The Hon. Member then referred, as I understand him, to some award of costs against the federal Government and in favour of some independent dealers. It would seem that this is not a tax matter. It is just another example of members having before them a few evasive facts of a case and then drawing conclusions which are often erroneous. I invite all Hon. Members, in situations where they deem that their constituents have been unfairly treated by the Department, to bring the matter to the Minister's attention with all the details-and I stress all the details-pertaining to the case.
